content:
Hi! My question will reveal my OCaml/Standard ML/Rocq background.

I am formalizing papers in CS where there are plenty of definitions and statements that are to be manually checked and trusted by the user, and plenty more of definitions that are used only in proofs and require no checks.

What I would do in a system with module types is to have a final Paper module type interface that imports only files containing the trusted definitions used in the statements and that lists all theorems whose statement is to be checked as fields of the module type. Then I will have a module type implementation tha imports all the stuff needed.

I don't know of a way to achieve the same in Lean: I can write a Paper.lean file/module, state everything and use as proofs just "exacts" referring to the proofs in other files, and that's what I do indeed. However, I am forced to import at the beginning of the file all the lean files that are required by the proofs. Therefore it is not obvious which definitions are to be checked by the user and which don't.

Am I missing some feature of Lean here? The only workaround that comes to my mind is very ugly: collect all statements together in a struct declaration that plays the role of the module interface. Not very nice when I have tens (or hundreds) of statements.

Thank you both, no, I was not aware of Comparator. It solves the problem indeed.

I must also notice that it is quite a cognitively heavy solution: to convince a reviewer of the paper that it works you need to let him understand the difference between the challenge and the solution files ("why are there sorry left in challenge while you claim the proofs are sorry free?"), how to run the comparator, what it does, etc. Module type interfaces a la ML are sexier :-)
